documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: Generative AI Policy for Students (August 2023)
documents.stance_why: The policy says use 'in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member' is an Honor Code violation, so AI is off unless the instructor allows it, while it also praises supportive uses. That is restrict rather than delegates, because it fixes a default.
documents.summary: The university-wide student policy from the Office of Academic Standards. It praises AI for brainstorming, study aids and concept help but frames misuse as replacing learning, and declares work AI-generated or modified and passed off as one's own to be dishonest. Use not expressly permitted by the instructor is an Honor Code violation.

units.why: The policy names study guides and practice problems as supportive uses: 'making study guides or practice problems'. This is a permission for study aids, so P14.
units.anchor: making study guides or practice problems

units.why: The same sentence lists 'thinking through ideas' as a way AI supports education, which is idea generation, so P15.
units.anchor: thinking through ideas

units.why: It lists 'help with understanding difficult concepts' as a legitimate support, matching the concept-tutor type P12.
units.anchor: help with understanding difficult concepts

units.why: The passage gives the reason for limits: using AI 'as a substitute for genuine engagement' undermines learning, which is the skill-building rationale P41, not a fairness rationale.
units.anchor: substitute for genuine engagement, or to circumvent the necessary intellectual challenges

units.why: It asks students to keep AI as a supplement, not a replacement for their own thinking: 'supplementing your education and replacing it'. Closest is P32 (student stays the primary thinker).
units.anchor: the difference between supplementing your education and replacing it

units.why: The policy states its purpose is 'not to be overly punitive' but to ensure deep engagement, an educative framing of enforcement (P68).
units.anchor: not to be overly punitive
units.fit_note: Framed as the purpose of the policy rather than a rule about responding to a particular case.

units.why: The sentence acknowledges that 'you will most likely use it in your chosen field', a professional-readiness argument that AI matters for careers (P44), though it does not say courses teach it.
units.anchor: you will most likely use it in your chosen field
units.fit_note: Acknowledges AI in future careers but does not say courses teach AI use.

units.why: AI is limited so that students 'acquire the knowledge and skills that your assignments are meant to produce'; this is the skill-building rationale, P41.
units.anchor: acquire the knowledge and skills that your assignments are meant to produce

units.why: The sentence classes passing off AI-generated or AI-modified work as one's own as 'academic dishonesty'. I chose P36 (classification as misconduct) over P19 because the sentence defines the offence rather than listing a banned use.
units.anchor: including work generated or materially modified by AI, constitutes academic dishonesty

units.why: Use that violates 'an instructor's articulated policy' is an Honor Code violation, which classifies misuse as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: violates an instructor’s articulated policy

units.why: Use 'not expressly permitted by the faculty member' is a violation, so the fallback when the instructor is silent is no AI: P06. Different from P36 because it sets the default.
units.anchor: in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member

units.why: Students with questions are directed to a named office, 'the Office of Academic Standards', i.e. human help (P72).
units.anchor: please contact the Office of Academic Standards
units.fit_note: Directs to an office for policy questions, not to instructors or writing support.

documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: Statement on Generative AI and Academic Integrity (May 2023)
documents.stance_why: The statement says 'the authority to define the appropriate use ... rests with the faculty' and gives prohibit or encourage as examples, so the document sets no stance itself and delegates.
documents.summary: A May 2023 university statement that leaves AI rules to faculty, who may ban or encourage it. Instructors must communicate expectations; students must not pass off AI-generated work as their own, and violations go through the Honor Code procedures.

units.why: The statement says 'we want to embrace every available tool' and that technology 'provides new opportunities', naming benefits without setting a rule (P87).
units.anchor: we want to embrace every available tool that will aid in this educational journey

units.why: Replacing 'the rigorous demands of and personal engagement with their coursework' is said to undermine education; it is the skill-building rationale P41.
units.anchor: to replace the rigorous demands of and personal engagement with their coursework

units.why: The university hands the decision to faculty: 'authority to define the appropriate use ... rests with the faculty'. That is P04.
units.anchor: the authority to define the appropriate use, study, and deployment of these technologies

units.why: Instructors 'may choose to prohibit or strictly manage' AI, e.g. in an intro writing course. It permits an instructor-set ban, so P04.
units.anchor: an instructor may choose to prohibit or strictly manage the use of these technologies

units.why: Instructors may instead 'encourage the use of these technologies as part of a creative process'; the choice is the instructor's (P04).
units.anchor: an instructor might encourage the use of these technologies as part of a creative process

units.why: Instructors must tell students their course expectations: 'responsibility is to communicate'. P09 (state AI expectations) fits; no syllabus is named, so a small gap.
units.anchor: the instructor's responsibility is to communicate to students the expectations for their course
units.fit_note: Does not say where (syllabus) the expectations are stated.

units.why: Students must 'never' pass off work they did not produce, including AI-generated or modified work: ownership of submitted work (P29).
units.anchor: never to represent work they did not produce as their own

units.why: Violations go to 'the procedures and remedies outlined in the Procedural Appendix', administered by the Office of Academic Standards: a formal procedure (P81).
units.anchor: the procedures and remedies outlined in the Procedural Appendix to the Honor Code

documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: Policy Update: AI Editing Tools (Fall 2024)
documents.stance_why: The update sets no stance of its own: it says 'if your instructor prohibits the use of gen AI ... this prohibition includes the use of editing tools', extending whatever the instructor decides.
documents.summary: A Fall 2024 Honor Code update clarifying that AI editing tools such as Grammarly count as generative AI, so an instructor's prohibition covers them unless stated otherwise. It warns about detector flags and unattributed AI suggestions, and tells students to check the syllabus or ask.

units.why: Defines AI editing tools as tools that 'suggest revisions' and so produce 'AI-generated text', which sets what the policy covers (P61).
units.anchor: AI-powered editing tools like Grammarly and WordTune

units.why: A prohibition 'includes the use of editing tools', so AI proofreading is banned where AI is. P21 (no AI to proofread or check graded work) fits best.
units.anchor: this prohibition includes the use of editing tools, unless explicitly stated otherwise

units.why: Warns that detectors flag even minimal editing-tool help; it concerns detector use (P40) but gives a warning, not a rule.
units.anchor: even a small number of suggestions from an AI editing tool
units.fit_note: Says detectors will flag editing-tool text and that this is not a false positive; it does not tell instructors to use detectors.

units.why: Using AI suggestions 'without proper attribution' is academic dishonesty: nondisclosure is the violation (P28), not just a disclosure duty (P24).
units.anchor: using AI-generated suggestions without proper attribution can be considered a form of academic dishonesty

units.why: When unsure, students 'check the syllabus or ask your instructor' (P10; the syllabus check resembles P78 but the ask is the main rule).
units.anchor: ask your instructor for clarification

units.why: Students should 'consider citing the use' of permitted editing tools, a soft disclosure recommendation (P24).
units.anchor: consider citing the use of these tools if they are allowed

documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: AI Recommendations for Instructors
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors to 'be explicit with students about your expectations' and supplies sample statements from ban to 'generally acceptable', so the stance rests with instructors.
documents.summary: Honor Code office recommendations for instructors: warn students that chatbots are unreliable, state expectations in the syllabus and Canvas, and treat unauthorized use as an Honor Code violation. It offers four sample statements ranging from a ban to attributed use, and urges instructors to try the tools and discuss them.

units.why: Instructors are told to remind students that the tools 'do not meet the standards' of academic work, citing hallucinations and missing citations: AI output is unreliable (P31).
units.anchor: Remind students that ChatGPT and related tools do not meet the standards

units.why: Names 'the lack of accountability for the ethical and equitable sourcing of information' as a known problem with the tools, an ethical concern (P53).
units.anchor: the lack of accountability for the ethical and equitable sourcing of information

units.why: Argues that critical thinking and writing are 'the hard but essential core' of the education, a skill-building reason for care with AI (P41).
units.anchor: form the hard but essential core of a liberal arts education

units.why: Instructors should 'be explicit with students about your expectations' for assignments, exams and class: communicate AI rules (P09).
units.anchor: Be explicit with students about your expectations regarding the use of ChatGPT

units.why: Instructors should make clear that 'unauthorized use ... will be considered a violation of the Honor Code': misconduct classification (P36).
units.anchor: unauthorized use of generative AI will be considered a violation of the Honor Code

units.why: Editing tools like Grammarly count under a prohibition: AI proofreading/revising is banned where AI is (P21).
units.anchor: This includes AI editing tools (such as Grammarly)

units.why: Instructors are advised to add 'a specific statement in your syllabus and on Canvas': syllabus AI statement (P09, as a recommendation).
units.anchor: Consider adding a specific statement in your syllabus and on Canvas

units.why: The page supplies four sample syllabus statements for instructors to adapt (P110).
units.anchor: The following sample statements may be helpful in crafting statements

units.why: The sample statement says students 'signed the Honor Code pledge' and that this includes appropriate generative AI use; it ties the pledge to AI (P111).
units.anchor: you signed the Honor Code pledge

units.why: Sample 1: AI composition and editing tools banned 'unless it is specifically permitted for the assignment', a default ban with exceptions (P01).
units.anchor: you may not use any generative AI composition or editing tools

units.why: Sample 2 sets the silent-assignment default as no AI: 'unless specifically stated in the assignment' (P06).
units.anchor: may not be used for assignments in this course unless specifically stated in the assignment

units.why: Where AI use is permitted, content 'must be properly attributed': disclosure with the submission (P24).
units.anchor: the content generated or modified by AI must be properly attributed

units.why: Sample 3 makes AI 'generally acceptable', a permit-by-default rule (P02).
units.anchor: The use of AI tools is generally acceptable in this course

units.why: Reproducible attribution lists 'the date accessed, the web address ... and a description of the prompt': specific citation details (P25).
units.anchor: the date accessed, the web address or URL accessed, and a description of the prompt

units.why: Students are 'responsible for assessing the quality, completeness, and accuracy' of AI information: verify output (P31).
units.anchor: you are responsible for assessing the quality, completeness, and accuracy

units.why: Sample 4: students 'will be required to describe the uses and process' where assignments allow AI, a description/reflection requirement (P26).
units.anchor: you will be required to describe the uses and process

units.why: Instructors are told to 'become familiar with ChatGPT', supporting their own learning (P63).
units.anchor: Become familiar with ChatGPT and related tools

units.why: Instructors should 'engage with colleagues, students, and others in dialogue' about AI use and misuse. Nearest is P66 (discuss AI with students), though colleagues are included too.
units.anchor: Engage with colleagues, students, and others in dialogue
units.fit_note: Also covers dialogue with colleagues and the disciplines, not only with students.

units.why: Instructors should 'put your assignments into the system to see how it responds', testing assignments against AI; this is a way to learn the tools (P63).
units.anchor: put your assignments into the system to see how it responds
units.fit_note: Specifically about testing one's own assignments against AI.

units.why: Predicts AI will be 'embedded within the common applications' students use. It is a forecast, not a rule on embedded-tool use, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: pervasive, ubiquitous, and embedded within the common applications
units.uncovered_note: Forecast that AI will become pervasive and embedded in everyday applications, offered as context for rethinking teaching.

units.why: Warns that asking ChatGPT whether it wrote a text is unreliable: do not use the chatbot as a detector (P39).
units.anchor: ChatGPT does not know whether it wrote a particular piece of text
units.fit_note: Concerns asking the chatbot itself, not detector software.

documents.title: Establishing AI Policies for Your Course (Syllabus Policy Language)
documents.stance_why: The guide offers a 'Closed/Strategic/Open framework' and tells faculty to choose one for their course ('selecting one of the following approaches'), so it lists tiers and decides nothing itself.
documents.summary: A Notre Dame Learning guide to writing syllabus AI policies at university, course and assignment levels. It presents three stances with sample wording and examples, and adds advice on cost, opt-out, privacy, accessibility and verification.

units.why: Argues a 'clear AI policy in your syllabus' removes guesswork; as guidance to put an AI statement in the syllabus, P09.
units.anchor: A clear AI policy in your syllabus takes away the guesswork

units.why: Policies are set at three levels, university, course, assignment, and the instructor decides at the lower two: let each course and assignment set the rule (P04).
units.anchor: aligning with University guidance, setting a course-level stance, and clarifying details for each assignment

units.why: Instructors should 'align your course policy with University Honor Code language'. P109 (coordinate rules) is the nearest; the alignment is with the university, not colleagues.
units.anchor: align your course policy with University Honor Code language
units.fit_note: Alignment is with the university-level Honor Code language, not with other sections or departments.

units.why: Syllabi should 'link to the Honor Code and any campus AI guidance', pointing students to further resources (P115).
units.anchor: Link to the Honor Code and any campus AI guidance

units.why: The course layer should 'state your general stance' in the syllabus: a syllabus AI statement (P09).
units.anchor: State your general stance and the rationale tied to learning outcomes in your syllabus

units.why: The rationale is to be 'tied to learning outcomes', aligning AI decisions with objectives (P83).
units.anchor: the rationale tied to learning outcomes

units.why: At assignment level, instructors 'specify what's allowed for this task ... and the required disclosure format': per-assignment statement (P09).
units.anchor: what must be cited, and the required disclosure format

units.why: Names a local 'Closed/Strategic/Open framework' of three stances for courses: named tiers (P05).
units.anchor: Closed/Strategic/Open framework

units.why: Closed model sample: AI 'may not be used for any part of this course', a total ban (P01).
units.anchor: may not be used for any part of this course

units.why: The closed sample ends 'Ask if you are unsure'; students ask the instructor (P10).
units.anchor: Ask if you are unsure

units.why: The closed example checks understanding by 'a brief oral check ... explaining one step of their reasoning' (P34).
units.anchor: a brief oral check (five minutes in office hours or Zoom)

units.why: Strategic sample: AI 'for brainstorming and outlining only' limits AI to a closed list of tasks (P107); brainstorming alone would be P15, but 'only' makes it a task limit.
units.anchor: for brainstorming and outlining only

units.why: Strategic sample: 'Directly pasted AI text is not permitted', so AI may not produce the submitted text (P19).
units.anchor: Directly pasted AI text is not permitted

units.why: The 'AI use' note must list 'the tool, date, prompt(s), and how you used the output': specific citation details (P25).
units.anchor: list the tool, date, prompt(s), and how you used the output

units.why: Open sample: students are 'encouraged to use generative AI as a collaborator', an encourage-by-default rule (P02).
units.anchor: You are encouraged to use generative AI as a collaborator

units.why: Open sample: 'You remain responsible for accuracy, originality, and citation', ownership (P29).
units.anchor: You remain responsible for accuracy, originality, and citation

units.why: Open sample: quoted or closely paraphrased AI output must be marked and attributed (P24).
units.anchor: mark it as such and provide attribution

units.why: The software-studio example invites AI to 'refactor code or generate tests': AI-generated code allowed under conditions (P16).
units.anchor: use AI to refactor code or generate tests

units.why: The example pairs AI use with 'a repository log and a reflective memo': logs and reflections (P26).
units.anchor: a repository log and a reflective memo on what they accepted or rejected and why

units.why: Instructors should 'provide no-cost or institutionally supported options': equitable access (P51).
units.anchor: Provide no-cost or institutionally supported options when feasible

units.why: Instructors should 'accept non-AI pathways for students who opt out': alternatives keep access equitable (P51).
units.anchor: Accept non-AI pathways for students who opt out

units.why: Do not require 'sensitive or proprietary data' uploads to public tools; prompts may be retained: data protection (P50).
units.anchor: Avoid requiring students to upload sensitive or proprietary data to public tools

units.why: Asks for 'captioning and screen-reader compatibility in AI-enabled workflows': accessibility (P97).
units.anchor: ensure captioning and screen-reader compatibility in AI-enabled workflows

units.why: Instructors should 'teach verification: fact-check AI outputs': verify output (P31).
units.anchor: Fact-check AI outputs, check citations

units.why: Instructors should 'communicate your policy clearly in your syllabus and on the first day of class': communicating expectations (P09).
units.anchor: on the first day of class

units.why: Instructors are directed to 'seek support from ND Learning': faculty support for AI policy (P63).
units.anchor: Seek support from ND Learning or your colleagues

documents.unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
documents.title: CSE Guide to the Honor Code
documents.stance_why: The guide says 'in every course, the instructor has the final say' and only describes how to think about sources; it fixes no AI rule of its own beyond treating AI output as 'the work of another'.
documents.summary: The CSE department's guide to the Honor Code, built on worked ChatGPT examples that separate consulting from copying and resources from solutions. Instructors decide what is allowed; the guide covers citation, code marking, and reporting.

units.why: The department guide yields to instructors: 'the instructor has the final say' (P04).
units.anchor: in every course, the instructor has the final say about expectations of academic honesty

units.why: All CSE students are 'expected to abide by' the Honor Code pledge, which the guide applies to AI sources; P111 (pledge).
units.anchor: expected to abide by the Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor Pledge
units.fit_note: Pledge is a general honor-code pledge, not AI-specific.

units.why: Output 'should be regarded as the work of another, not your own' treats AI like another person under existing rules (P45).
units.anchor: the output of these systems should be regarded as the work of another

units.why: Sets scope: the ChatGPT examples apply to 'any model of this kind' (P61).
units.anchor: should be understood to apply to any model of this kind

units.why: The guide treats sources uniformly, yet 'instructors may have different policies for different kinds of sources' (P04).
units.anchor: instructors may have different policies for different kinds of sources

units.why: A syllabus might set each activity as 'allowed, allowed only with proper citation, or not allowed': a table of uses with levels (P05).
units.anchor: declare whether that activity is allowed, allowed only with proper citation, or not allowed

units.why: Warns the sample policy 'should not be assumed as default', so students cannot presume a default; closest is P06 (silent-syllabus fallback), but it states there is none.
units.anchor: should not be assumed as default
units.fit_note: It denies any default rather than naming one.

units.why: The worked example lists asking ChatGPT to explain quicksort without code as consulting a resource, which the common policy allows (P12).
units.anchor: Please explain quicksort to me, without writing code
units.fit_note: Illustrates a use via example rather than stating a permission outright.

units.why: Asking a syntax question, reading the answer and closing the window is listed as consulting; closing before writing fits P23 (keep AI apart from the work).
units.anchor: read the answer, and close the window
units.fit_note: Example of acceptable consulting; includes asking a syntax question as well as closing the window.

units.why: Listed as copying a solution, which the example policy does not allow ('Copying not allowed'): having AI write the submitted code (P19).
units.anchor: Please implement quicksort in C
units.fit_note: Stated as a worked example, whose prohibition follows from the sample homework policy.

units.why: Defines 'solution' and 'resource', the terms used to judge sources including AI (P61).
units.anchor: A source that partially or totally fulfills that requirement is a solution

units.why: Warns the systems 'can easily cross over the line from resource to solution'; no listed type covers this risk of unintended overreach.
units.anchor: can easily cross over the line from resource to solution
units.uncovered_note: Warns that AI tends to give more help than asked for, so students must watch the line between resource and solution.

units.why: When in doubt, 'you should ask your instructor' (P10).
units.anchor: you should ask your instructor

units.why: Words or ideas of another, including AI treated as a source, must be properly cited: cite AI use (P24).
units.anchor: you must properly cite them

units.why: States that 'standards for citation of generative AI systems are still evolving': provisional rules (P54).
units.anchor: Standards for citation of generative AI systems are still evolving
units.fit_note: Says the citation standards are evolving, not that this policy will be revised.

units.why: The citation must identify the source and 'what part of the assignment you were working on'; specific details (P25).
units.anchor: indicate what part of the assignment you were working on

units.why: Copied code must be marked with comments at the exact place, with a ChatGPT example in the guide: mark AI-derived code (P27).
units.anchor: use comments to mark off exactly which lines, functions, or files are reused

units.why: Instructors 'may (but [are] not required to) give a warning' for borderline conduct, a lighter, educative step before formal action (P68).
units.anchor: he or she may (but is not required to) give a warning
units.fit_note: A warning for borderline behavior, not stated as a first-offence policy.

units.why: For conduct judged dishonest the instructor 'is required to file' a report: a formal reporting procedure (P81).
units.anchor: he or she is required to file either an Honor Code Violation Report

notes: Coder A. No course layer collected (deferred). The Aug 2023 Generative AI Policy for Students is the university anchor; the CSE guide is a department honor-code guide that applies it.
